entry.title: Quaternions
entry.content:
I took some robotics classes recently and although our professor only stuck to Euler angles, I couldn’t help but explore the rich world of quaternions. I hope this resultant writeup is somewhat helpful in understanding quaternions, particularly from the perspective of linear algebra.

Two Dimensional Rotations

Let us start with the familiar rotations in two dimensional plane. A point $(x, y)$ is to be rotated $\theta$ around the origin.
The basis vectors are sent to \(\hat{i}_{rotated} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\hat{j}_{rotated} = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin\theta \\ \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\)

The first identity is easy to see from the very definitions of trigonometric functions. The second follows from $+90 ^\circ$ rotation of the first point.
Then general rotation is then defined by the linear transformation:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta \\ x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\]

Equivalently we can also employ complex numbers to represent rotations. Complex numbers are formed by pairs of reals $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ to get $a+bi$, where $i^2 = -1$. The squared magnitude of complex number is defined as $a^2+b^2$.
If we then define complex multiplication with the usual distributive law, we can show that multiplication by complex number whose magnitude is $1$ corresponds to rotation of the number when interpreted as a two dimensional point.
i.e.

\[(a+bi)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta) = (a\cos\theta-b\sin\theta) + (a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta)i\]

We can also use matrices to represent complex numbers such that matrix multiplication corresponds to complex numbers multiplication. Specifically, write

\[R_\theta = \cos\theta\,\mathbf{1} +\sin\theta\,\mathbf{i}\]

where the identity matrix is denoted as $\mathbf{1}$ and the $+90^\circ$ rotation matrix as $\mathbf{i}$:

\[\mathbf{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \mathbf{i} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Here our general rotation matrix $R_\theta$ belongs to the vector space of all $2\times2$ matrices that represent rotations, whose basis vectors are $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{i}$. Verify that these basis vectors are orthogonal to each other. From here on, it will be helpful to think all the matrices as a long vector.
Each rotation can thus be thought of as being composed of a $\cos\theta$ component of $0^\circ$ rotation and a $\sin\theta$ component of $+90^\circ$ rotation (these projections can also be obtained by dot product with the basis vectors if they are unit magnitudes, which we can achieve by dividing by $\sqrt2$, but lets avoid that ugliness for now). Not just rotation matrices but any general complex number $a+bi$ has a matrix representation

\[\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix}\]

We can verify that its determinant corresponds to the squared magnitude of the complex number and matrix multiplication corresponds to complex number multiplication. So we can establish multiplicative law for complex number magnitudes from the corresponding law for determinants.
i.e.

\[|xy| = |x||y|\]

The fact that complex numbers multiplication corresponds to rotation in plane can also be established from its properties that the multiplication is distributive and that magnitudes get multiplied.
Say $u$ is a complex number with magnitude $1$ and $v$ and $w$ are any two complex numbers.
Then, distance between $uv$ and $uw$ is:

\[\begin{aligned} &|uv-uw| \\ &=|u(v-w)| \\ &= |u||v-w| \\ &= |v-w| \end{aligned}\]

Thus the transformation preserves distance while sending origin to itself. Also if $u \neq 1$ then no other point is stationary and the effect is thus rotation.

Quaternions

We can now start our investigation in higher dimension by asking if we can find three dimensional numbers with these properties so that multiplication represents similar isometric transformations. It turns out no such numbers exist in three dimensions but they do exist in four dimensions. They are called quaternions and are defined as:

\[x = a\mathbf{1} + b \mathbf{i} + c \mathbf{j} + d \mathbf{k}\]

where,

\[\mathbf{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{i} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{j} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ -i & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{k} = \begin{bmatrix} i & 0 \\ 0 & -i \end{bmatrix}\]

Note $i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = -1$
and $ij =k , jk = i, ki = j$
and $ij = -ji$ and so on so that multiplication is not commutative.

The basis vectors are again orthogonal to each other. The squared magnitude of the quaternion is $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ which can again be shown to be equal to the determinant of the corresponding matrix. From the matrix definitions, we can also see that the multiplicative property for absolute values holds. Thus, following a derivation similar to the two dimensional case, we can conclude that multiplication by unit quaternions represents an isometry of the $\mathbb{R^4}$ space. It still remains to be seen how to represent isometry of the $\mathbb{R}^3$ space.

Some Identities

First, let us play around with some properties of quaternions.
Define the quaternion conjugate $\bar{x}$ as $a \mathbf{1}-b \mathbf{i} - c \mathbf{j} - d \mathbf{k}$ and call a quaternion pure if $a=0$.
Then,
\(x\bar{x} = (a \mathbf{1} + b \mathbf{i} +c \mathbf{j} + d \mathbf{k})(a \mathbf{1} - b \mathbf{i} - c \mathbf{j} -d \mathbf{k}) = a^2+ b^2+c^2+d^2 = 1\)

for unit quaternions and

\[x^2 = (a \mathbf{1} + b \mathbf{i} +c \mathbf{j} + d \mathbf{k})^2 = a^2-b^2-c^2-d^2 = -|x|^2\]

for pure quaternions.

Note that in both expansions, all the terms where the quaternion terms differ cancels with its negative counterpart. For example $bc\mathbf{ij}$ cancels with $- bc \mathbf{ij}$ in the first expansion and $bc \mathbf{ij}$ cancels with $bc \mathbf{ji}$ in the second expansion. Particularly, for the unit quaternion, the conjugate also represents its inverse.
We can also obtain the following for pure quaternions:

\[\begin{alignat*}{2} && (a+b)^2 &= a^2 + ab + ba + b^2 \\ \implies && -|a+b|^2 &= a^2 + ab + ba + b^2 \\ \implies && -|a|^2 - 2 \langle a, b \rangle - |b|^2 &= -|a|^2 + ab + ba - |b|^2 \\ \implies && ab + ba &= -2 \langle a, b \rangle \end{alignat*}\]

Particularly, $ab = -ba$ if $a$ and $b$ are perpendicular.

Pure Quaternions induce Quarter Rotations

We already know that quaternions represent isometries in the $\mathbb{R}^4$ space. To somehow extract three dimensional rotation from this isometry, we will first characterize multiplication by a pure unit quaternion $\mathbf{u}$ by looking at action of $J(x) : x \mapsto \mathbf{u}x$ on different subspaces.
Specifically it is helpful to factor the space of quaternions $\mathbb{H}$ as:

\[\mathbb{H} = \text{span}(\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{u}) \oplus \mathbf{u}^\perp\]

The subspace spanned by $\mathbf{1}$ gets mapped by $J$ to the subspace spanned by $\mathbf{u}$ and vice versa. Now consider, within the pure quaternion subspace, the subspace perpendicular to $\mathbf{u}$ i.e. $\mathbf{u}^\perp$. Note that we are not including the subspace spanned by $\mathbf{1}$ in $\mathbf{u}^\perp$ for notational simplicity i.e. vectors in $\mathbf{u}^\perp$ are pure quaternions and form a two dimensional subspace.
For $x \in \mathbf{u}^\perp$, we can show that $\mathbf{u}x$ is still perpendicular to $\mathbf{u}$ by noting that

\[\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{u}x) = \mathbf{u}^2x = -x \quad\quad\quad\quad (\mathbf{u}x)\mathbf{u} = -(xu)\mathbf{u} = x\]

where we used $\mathbf{u}x = -x\mathbf{u}$ since $\mathbf{u}\perp x$. Thus elements in the plane $\mathbf{u}^\perp$ are mapped to itself, and furthermore the transformation is distance preserving, so that the net effect is rotation of the plane. To calculate the angle of rotation note that applying the left-multiplication by $\mathbf{u}$ twice i.e.

\[\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{u}x) = -x\]

corresponds to $180^\circ$ rotation, so that a single multiplication must correspond to $90^\circ$ rotation. We don’t know if the direction of rotation is $+90^\circ$ (anti-clockwise) or $-90^\circ$ (clockwise) rotation about $\mathbf{u}$. The direction of rotation is in fact fixed by the handedness of our co-ordinate system. To find this direction, we can simply look at the special case when $\mathbf{u} = i$ and note that $ij = k$, which means with our right-handed $ijk$ co-ordinate system, the rotation must be $+90^\circ$. Thus, the vectors $x \in \mathbf{u}^\perp$ are mapped to $J(x) \in \mathbf{u}^\perp$ with $J(x) \perp x$.

Three Dimensional Rotations with General Quaternions

If we recall how we composed a general rotation for the two dimensional case as combination of the cosine of identity transformation and sine of $90^\circ$ rotation, we might be motivated to look at multiplication by a general unit quaternion $t = \cos\theta\mathbf{1} + \sin\theta\mathbf{u}$ where $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit pure quaternion.
Let us similarly look at the action of transformation $T(x) = tx$ on different subspaces.
For $\text{span}(\mathbf{1})$, the basis vector $\mathbf{1}$ is sent to $\cos\theta\mathbf{1}+\sin\theta\mathbf{u}$.
For $\text{span}(\mathbf{u})$, the basis vector $\mathbf{u}$ is sent to $-\sin\theta\mathbf{1}+\cos\theta\mathbf{u}$.
For $x \in \mathbf{u}^\perp$,

\[\begin{aligned} T(x) &= (\cos\theta\mathbf{1}+\sin\theta\mathbf{u})x \\ &= (\cos\theta x+\sin\theta J(x)) \\ \end{aligned}\]

Thus, the operation $T$ describes a rotation by $\theta$ in the $\text{span}(\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{u}$) plane and a rotation by $\theta$ in the $\mathbf{u}^\perp$ plane. This is nearly what we want.
The rotation by $\theta$ in the $\mathbf{u}^\perp$ plane is particularly interesting. The points in this space get rotated angle $\theta$ around the axis defined by $\mathbf{u}$. If we could do this for not just the elements of $\mathbf{u}^\perp$ but for the whole pure quaternion space: $\text{span}(\mathbf{u}) \oplus \mathbf{u}^\perp$, we will have achieved our objective (where we would interpret a three dimensional rotation axis as a pure quaternion for computation).
You might have already noticed that this is possible by projecting a given vector $x$ to $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{u}^\perp$, rotating the component perpendicular to $\mathbf{u}$ by left multiplication as above and adding back the component parallel to $\mathbf{u}$. Indeed this works and will give you the correct vector. But we still need a bit of work to arrive at the more commonly expressed form of quaternion multiplication for rotation.

We can begin by looking for a transformation that will cancel the effect for $\text{span}(\mathbf{u})$ while hopefully preserving the effect for $\mathbf{u}^\perp$. And indeed, with a bit of playing around one might arrive at the map

\[U(x) = xt^{-1} = x(\cos\theta\mathbf{1}-\sin\theta\mathbf{u})\]

whose effects for the considered subspaces are:
For $\text{span}(\mathbf{1})$, the basis vector $\mathbf{1}$ is sent to $\cos\theta\mathbf{1}-\sin\theta\mathbf{u}$.
For $\text{span}(\mathbf{u})$, the basis vector $\mathbf{u}$ is sent to $\sin\theta\mathbf{1}+\cos\theta\mathbf{u}$.
For $x \in \mathbf{u}^\perp$,

\[\begin{aligned} U(x) &= x(\cos\theta\mathbf{1}-\sin\theta\mathbf{u}) \\ &= (\cos\theta x-\sin\theta x\mathbf{u}) \\ &= (\cos\theta x+\sin\theta \mathbf{u}x) \\ \end{aligned}\]

where the last equality follows from $\mathbf{u}x = -x\mathbf{u}$ since $x\perp \mathbf{u}$.
Thus, this map rotates the $\text{span}(\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{u}$) plane by $-\theta$ i.e. in the opposite direction as $T$ and rotates the $\mathbf{u}^\perp$ plane by $\theta$ in the same direction as $T$.
If we compose these maps, we get $V(x) = txt^{-1}$, whose net effect is the identity transformation for $\text{span}(\mathbf{1}, u)$ and $2\theta$ rotation about the axis $\mathbf{u}$ for $\mathbf{u}^\perp$. Thus, for any vector represented as a pure quaternion $x$, it would have its $\mathbf{u}^\parallel$ and $\mathbf{u}^\perp$ components transformed so that the vector $x$ is rotated by angle $2\theta$ around the $\mathbf{u}$ axis.

Final Algorithm

To conclude, we state the algorithm for general rotation of vector $v$ about an axis $u$ by angle $\alpha$ below:

  1. Represent $v$ as a pure quaternion.
  2. Define quaternion $t = \cos\frac{\alpha}{2} + \mathbf{u}\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}$ where $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit pure quaternion representation of axis $u$.
  3. Compute rotated quaternion $v’=tvt^{-1}$ following the algebraic rules for quaternion multiplication.
entry.summary: A Linear Algebraic Approach to Quaternions

entry.title: Flow Matching
entry.content:
This write-up is primarily based on the excellent lecture-notes, which I encourage the readers to check out. I have tried to condense the content and simplify some derivations. I expect to follow up with a separate write-up on Diffusion and SDE.

Setup

We want to model some data generating distribution $p_{data}$ using samples $(y_1, y_2, …, y_n)$ drawn from this distribution. We will do so by defining a map from samples from some simple distribution $p_{\text{init}}$ (for example, a gaussian distribution with zero mean and unit covariance matrix) to samples from our data generating distribution $p_{data}$. Towards this, we will define a family of intermediate variables $x_t$ drawn from distributions $p_t$ where $p_0 = p_{\text{init}}$ and $p_1 = p_{data}$ for $t \in [0, 1]$. Note that $x_t$ is defined to have the same dimensionality as the data distribution. The trajectory of $x_t$ is defined using the ODE:

\[\frac{d}{dt}x_t = u_t(x_t)\]

where we want to learn $u_t$ such that drawing different samples $x_0$ from $p_{\text{init}}$ and following this ODE from $t = 0$ to $t = 1$ will lead to different samples from $p_{data}$.
Note that $u_t$ is time dependent and learns a function with same input/output dimensionality as the data. Thus, we can interpret it as learning a vector field in the data space which tells at each time how to nudge each point such that starting from points drawn from $p_{\text{init}}$ at $t = 0$ and evolving it to $t = 1$, we end up with different samples from $p_{data}$.
Here $u_t$ is said to describe a flow.

Sampling

If we have such a $u_t$ we can simulate it to draw samples from $p_{data}$, for example, using the Euler Method with:

\[\begin{aligned} x_0 &\sim p_{\text{init}}& \\ x_{t+h} &= x_t + h \cdot u_t(x_t) \quad\ \ t = [0, h, 2h, ..., (n-1)h] \end{aligned}\]

where $n$ is number of steps and $h=1/n$ is the step-size.
To learn such a $u_t$ we will try to explicitly construct a target $u_t$ which has this desired property.

Conditional Flow

First, instead of constructing flow for the whole data, we will construct flow for any single data-point $y$: $u_{t, y}$ such that evolving this flow from $t = 0$ to $t = 1$ will land us on $y$ for any $x_0$ drawn from $p_{\text{init}}$.

\[\begin{aligned} x_0 &\sim p_0 \\ \frac{d}{dt}x_t \quad&= u_{t,y}(x_t) \\ x_1 \quad&= y \end{aligned}\]

To construct this flow we can construct a set of conditional interpolating distributions $p(x_t \mid y)$ which describes the distribution of $x_t$ at each t. We have $p(x_0 \mid y)$ = $p_{\text{init}}$ and since $p(x_t \mid y)$ is concentrated on a single point y at $t = 1$, we can model this as a Dirac-Delta distribution $\delta(y)$. It is called conditional interpolating distribution because for a given $y$ it interpolates between $p_{\text{init}}$ and the sample $y$. We can use this later to construct a marginal interpolating distribution and the corresponding marginal flow which will interpolate between $p_{\text{init}}$ and $p_{data}$ as required.

Example

We can define an example conditional interpolating distribution using gaussian distribution as:

\[p(x_t|y) = \mathcal{N}(\alpha_t\ y, \beta_t\ I)\]

where $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ are defined such that

\[\begin{align*} \alpha_0 = 0 \quad \beta_0 = 1 \\ \alpha_1 = 1 \quad \beta_1 = 0 \end{align*}\]

Verify for yourself that $p_{\text{init}} := p(x_0 \mid y) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and $p(x_1 \mid y) = \delta(y)$.
We can now construct a conditional trajectory $x_t$ that each $x_0 \sim p_{\text{init}}$ takes such that $x_t$ will follow the conditional interpolating distribution $p(x_t \mid y)$ by defining the trajectory as:

\[x_t = \alpha_ty + \beta_tx_0\]

for each $x_0$
Since $x_0$ itself is normally distributed with zero mean and unit co-variance, you can verify for yourself that the defined $x_t$ will follow the required Normal distribution outlined above.
We simply have to take time derivative of this $x_t$ to get the conditional flow

\[u_{t,y}(x_t) = \frac{d}{dt}x_t = \dot{\alpha_t}y+\dot{\beta_t}x_0 = \dot{\alpha_t}y+\frac{\dot{\beta_t}}{\beta_t}(x_t - \alpha_ty))\]

Marginal Flow

Define marginal interpolating distribution of random variable $x_t$ as

\[p(x_t) = \int p(x_t|y)p_{data}(y) \, dy\]

i.e. to sample $x_t$, we sample $y$ from $p_{data}$, then we sample $x_t$ from $p(x_t \mid y)$. The resulting distribution of $x_t$ is defined as the marginal interpolating distribution.
We can verify that $p(x_0) = p_{\text{init}}$ and $p(x_1) = p_{data}$ using the definition of Dirac-Delta function. Thus, if we can construct a flow to follow this distribution, we can sample from the data distribution by simulating the ODE as outlined in the section Sampling.

Important Identity
It turns out that the marginal flow of this distribution can be defined in terms of conditional flow as:

\[u_t(x_t) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}(x_t)]\]

where $p(y \mid x_t)$ is the posterior distribution of $y$ given $x_t$, which using the Bayes rule, can be expressed as:

\[p(y|x_t) = \frac{p(x_t|y)\cdot p_{data}(y)}{p(x_t)}\]

For intuition, if we think about finitely many $y’s$, the marginal flow for $x_t$ can be obtained by averaging the conditional flow needed to reach $y$ over all the $y’s$ that $x_t$ could have come from. I hope this is somewhat intuitive, you can find the proof in the notes linked at the beginning.

Training Target

For any given $y$ we have seen how we can derive a conditional flow we want our model to approximate. For example, in the gaussian case we derived:

\[u_{t,y}^{target}(x_t) = \dot{\alpha_t}y+\frac{\dot{\beta_t}}{\beta_t}(x_t - \alpha_ty)\]

And the marginal flow we want to actually learn has the form:

\[u_t^{target}(x_t) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t)]\]

If we could calculate this, we could define the flow matching loss as:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ x_t \sim p(x_t)} \left\| u_t^{\text{target}}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t) \right\|^2 \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ x_t \sim p(x_t)} \left\| \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t)] - u_t^\theta(x_t) \right\|^2 \end{aligned}\]

That is for each timestep and $x_t$, try to match flow for $x_t$ against the target flow which is average of the conditional flow for all the $y$ the $x_t$ could have come from. Since we cannot easily sample from the posterior to estimate the inner expectation, we will apply the following trick to rewrite the loss as:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ x_t \sim p(x_t)} \left\| \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t)] - u_t^\theta(x_t) \right\|^2 \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ x_t \sim p(x_t)} \left\| \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t)] - \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_t^\theta(x_t)] \right\|^2 \end{aligned}\]

where, since the second term does not depend on $y$, rewriting it as expectation over $y$ makes no difference. Now the loss becomes,

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ x_t \sim p(x_t)} \left\| \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t)] \right\|^2 \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ x_t \sim p(x_t)}\left[ \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}\left\|u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t) \right\|^2 - \operatorname{Var}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t)]\right]\\ \end{aligned}\]

Here we used the identity $\operatorname{Var}[x] = \mathbb{E}[x^2]-\mathbb{E}[x]^2$ where $\operatorname{Var}[\cdot]$ denotes the element-wise variance of the vector-valued expression, i.e., the variance is computed independently for each coordinate of the vector. Furthermore, since the second term inside the variance: $u_{t}^{\theta}(x_t)$ does not depend on $y$, it works out as:

\[\operatorname{Var}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t)] = \operatorname{Var}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)}[u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t)]\]

which does not depend on the parameters $\theta$. Thus, we can omit this term and write the new loss with the squared term now inside the expectation as:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ x_t \sim p(x_t)}\left[ \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y|x_t)} \left\| u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t) \right\|^2 \right]\\ &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ x_t \sim p(x_t),\ y \sim p(y|x_t)} \left\| u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t) \right\|^2 \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [0,1],\ y \sim p_{data}(y),\ x_t \sim p(x_t|y)} \left\| u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t) \right\|^2 \\ \end{aligned}\]

where, for the final step, we rewrite the expectation over the joint distribution $p(x_t,y)$ as one over $y∼p(y)$, followed by $x_t∼p(x_t \mid y)$.
Notice that in the final form we don’t need to sample from the posterior distribution. Thus, we can train our model with minibatch gradient descent. We summarize the training and sampling algorithms in the following section.

Final Algorithm

Training Algorithm

Algorithm: Flow Matching Training
Given: Data distribution $p_{data}$, model $u_t^\theta$, and $p(x_t \mid y)$

For each mini-batch of data do:
    1. Sample $t \sim \left[0,1\right]$
    2. Sample $x_t \sim p(x_t \mid y)$
    3. Compute loss $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \lVert u_{t, y}^{target}(x_t) - u_t^\theta(x_t) \rVert^2$
    4. Update model parameters $\theta$ using gradient descent on loss $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$

Sampling Algorithm

Algorithm: Sampling from Flow Model
Given: Model $u_t^\theta$, number of steps $n$

  1. Set $t = 0$
  2. Set step-size $h = \frac{1}{n}$
  3. Sample $x_0 \sim p_{\text{init}}$
  4. for $i = 1, …, n$ do
      a. $x_{t+h} = x_t + h \cdot u_t(x_t)$
      b. $t = t + h$
  5. end for
  6. return $x_1$
